title: Pull, Draw, Drag
theme: The root tract: pulling and drawing
objectives: I can use the root tract (pull, draw) to work out the meaning of ten words.
I can explain how the prefixes dis-, sub-, ex-, re-, de-, con-, ab-, pro-, and in- change what tract means.
I can choose between close pairs such as retract and detract, or extract and subtract, using context.
I can write about a problem and its solution using words built on tract.
rationale: Tract carries one physical image, pulling, and the prefixes steer where the pull goes: away (distract, subtract, abstract), out (extract), back (retract), down or away (detract), together (contract), forward (protracted), and not (intractable). Students who hold that image can reason about words they have never met, which is the main reason this root opens the grade's word-part work. Several of the words are also multiple-meaning (extract, contract, abstract), so the unit pairs word-part analysis with careful sense choice. Traction and protracted give students two concrete-to-figurative moves: a grip on ice becomes support for an idea, and a pulled-out thread becomes a pulled-out dispute.

words.def: To pull someone's attention away from what they are trying to do.
words.ex: The buzzing phone began to distract Elena from her essay.
words.ex2: A magician waves one hand to distract the audience while the other hand does the trick.
words.nonExample: A teacher who waits until every eye is on her before speaking is not distracting the class.

apps.academic: Good study habits include removing anything that can distract you from the task.
apps.spoken: Sorry, I got distracted for a second. What did you say?
apps.writing: Use distract to show what keeps a character from noticing something important.

cloze.s: A loud construction crew outside began to ___ the students in the middle of the quiet reading test.

cloze2.s: The goalkeeper waved her arms behind the net to ___ the player lining up the penalty kick.

misuse.s: The librarian wanted to distract the readers, so she asked everyone to stay silent and concentrate on their books.
misuse.why: To distract is to pull attention away; asking for silence helps people concentrate.

visual.alt: A phone lighting up beside an open book.

words.frame: ___ can distract me when I am trying to ___.

words.def: To take one amount or number away from another.
words.ex: Subtract the cost of the ticket from your budget to see how much money is left.
words.ex2: The scorekeeper had to subtract two points after the referee reviewed the play.
words.nonExample: Putting five more dollars into the jar is not subtracting; it is the opposite operation.

apps.academic: In math, you subtract to find the difference between two numbers.
apps.spoken: If you subtract my share from the bill, we each owe the same.
apps.writing: Use subtract in a sentence about what is left after something is taken away.

cloze.s: To find your change, you must ___ the price of the snack from the ten dollars you handed over.

cloze2.s: The accountant had to ___ the shipping fees from the sales total before she could announce the true profit.

misuse.s: To find the total of the two scores, Kai subtracted them, and the number grew larger.
misuse.why: Subtracting takes an amount away, so the result gets smaller, not larger.

visual.alt: An abacus beside a minus sign.

words.frame: If I subtract ___ from ___, I am left with ___.

words.def: To pull or take something out, often with effort or care.

senses.def: A short passage taken from a longer piece of writing.
senses.example: The test began with a one-paragraph extract from a novel about a lighthouse keeper.

words.ex: The dentist had to extract the cracked tooth before it caused more pain.
words.ex2: Reporters tried to extract a clear answer from the mayor, but she kept changing the subject.
words.nonExample: Pushing a nail deeper into a board is the opposite of extracting it.

morph.note: The verb is stressed on the second syllable; the noun extract is stressed on the first.

apps.academic: In science, researchers extract a sample from a larger source before they test it.
apps.spoken: I couldn't extract a straight answer out of him.
apps.writing: Use extract when a character removes something with difficulty or patience.

cloze.s: With a pair of tweezers, the nurse carefully tried to ___ the tiny splinter from his thumb.

cloze2.s: Miners drill deep into the hillside to ___ copper from the hard rock.

misuse.s: The dentist extracted the tooth by gently pushing it deeper into the gum.
misuse.why: To extract is to pull something out, not to push it further in.

visual.alt: A pickaxe next to a gem that has been dug out of rock.

words.frame: It took effort to extract ___ from ___.

words.def: To take back something you said, or to pull something back in.
words.ex: The newspaper had to retract its story after the facts turned out to be wrong.
words.ex2: The cat retracted its claws and settled quietly into her lap.
words.nonExample: Repeating a claim louder after it has been proved false is not retracting it.

apps.academic: A scientific journal may retract a paper when its data prove unreliable.
apps.spoken: I retract what I said earlier; I had the date wrong.
apps.writing: Use retract when a speaker or writer takes back a statement in public.

cloze.s: After watching the video that proved him wrong, the senator was forced to ___ his statement.

cloze2.s: The pilot pressed a switch to ___ the landing gear into the belly of the plane once it was airborne.

misuse.s: The reporter retracted her article by repeating every claim again, even more loudly.
misuse.why: To retract is to take something back; repeating the claims is the opposite.

visual.alt: A newspaper beside an arrow curving backward.

words.frame: I would retract my statement about ___ because ___.

words.def: To make something seem less good or less valuable than it really is.
words.ex: A few spelling errors should not detract from the strength of your argument.
words.ex2: Bright billboards along the highway detract from the beauty of the valley.
words.nonExample: Fresh flowers on a table add to a room's charm; they do not detract from it.

apps.academic: Poor formatting can detract from an otherwise careful lab report.
apps.spoken: Don't let one mistake detract from everything you did right.
apps.writing: Use detract from to name the flaw that spoils the overall effect.

cloze.s: One small stain on the poster cannot ___ from the months of careful work you put into it.

cloze2.s: Critics said the clumsy special effects ___ from an otherwise gripping film.

misuse.s: The new mural detracts from the wall; everyone says it makes the school look better than ever.
misuse.why: To detract is to make something seem less good; praise for how the school looks shows the opposite.

visual.alt: A framed picture with a downward arrow beside it.

words.def: To shrink or draw together, becoming smaller or tighter.

senses.def: A written agreement that people are legally required to keep.
senses.example: The band signed a contract to play at the festival for three nights.

words.ex: Metal bridges contract slightly in winter and expand again in summer heat.
words.ex2: When you tighten your arm, the muscle contracts and bulges.
words.nonExample: A balloon that is being blown up is expanding, not contracting.

morph.note: The verb is stressed on the second syllable; the noun contract is stressed on the first.

apps.academic: Most materials contract when they cool and expand when they warm.
apps.spoken: My muscles contract when I'm cold and start to shiver.
apps.writing: Use contract for a physical shrinking, not for a signed agreement.

cloze.s: In the freezing night air, the metal rails slowly ___, leaving small gaps between the sections.

cloze2.s: As the cold water hit his skin, the muscles in his legs began to ___ and tighten.

misuse.s: The balloon contracted until it was twice its size and nearly burst.
misuse.why: To contract is to get smaller or tighter; growing bigger is the opposite.

visual.alt: An ice cube beside a ruler, showing something getting smaller in the cold.

words.def: Existing as an idea or quality rather than as a solid thing you can touch.

senses.def: A short summary of the main points of an article or report.
senses.example: Read the abstract first to decide whether the whole study is worth your time.

words.ex: Freedom is an abstract idea, so the class used pictures of flags and open gates to explain it.
words.ex2: Courage is easier to discuss when students tie the abstract word to a real story.
words.nonExample: A brick is not abstract; you can hold it in your hand.

morph.note: The prefix ab- is spelled abs- before t (ab -> abs).

apps.academic: Abstract nouns such as justice and honesty name ideas, not objects.
apps.spoken: That's a bit abstract for me; can you give a real example?
apps.writing: Support an abstract claim with a concrete detail so readers can picture it.

cloze.s: Instead of describing a real bridge, the teacher gave a purely ___ example: a rule about how forces behave.

cloze2.s: Justice, honesty, and friendship are ___ ideas; you cannot weigh them on a scale or hold them in your hand.

misuse.s: A rock is a perfect example of an abstract noun because you can pick it up and throw it.
misuse.why: Abstract words name ideas you cannot touch; a rock is a solid object.

visual.alt: A line from 'solid things you can touch' to 'ideas you cannot touch', with abstract near the idea end.

words.frame: An abstract idea such as ___ becomes clearer when I think of ___.

words.def: The grip a wheel or foot has on a surface, so that it does not slip.

senses.def: Support or forward progress that an idea or project begins to win.
senses.example: The petition gained traction when a local radio show mentioned it.

words.ex: Snow tires give a car better traction on icy roads.
words.ex2: Her soccer cleats dug into the wet grass and gave her enough traction to turn sharply.
words.nonExample: A tire spinning uselessly on ice has no traction at all.

apps.academic: Friction between a tire and the road is what gives a vehicle traction.
apps.spoken: My boots had no traction on the wet steps.
apps.writing: Use traction literally for grip, or figuratively for an idea that starts to catch on.

cloze.s: Sand spread across the icy driveway gave the tires enough ___ to climb the slope.

cloze2.s: Without ___ on the muddy trail, the hikers kept sliding backward with every step.

misuse.s: The bike had so much traction on the ice that its wheels spun helplessly in place.
misuse.why: Traction is grip; wheels that spin helplessly have none.

visual.alt: A car on a snowy road.

words.def: Lasting much longer than expected or needed; stretched out over a long time.
words.ex: After a protracted negotiation, the two sides finally agreed on a schedule.
words.ex2: Her protracted goodbye at the door made everyone late for the movie.
words.nonExample: A five-minute meeting that ends right on time is not protracted.

apps.academic: Historians describe protracted wars that lasted for decades.
apps.spoken: It was a protracted wait, and we were all tired of it.
apps.writing: Use protracted when length itself is part of the problem.

cloze.s: The ___ trial dragged on for fourteen months, far longer than anyone had predicted.

cloze2.s: After a ___ illness that kept her in bed all winter, Nora was glad to walk outside again.

misuse.s: The protracted meeting was over in thirty seconds.
misuse.why: Protracted means lasting a long time; thirty seconds is very short.

visual.alt: An hourglass beside a calendar full of crossed-out days.

words.frame: The protracted ___ lasted so long that ___.

words.def: Very hard to control, manage, or solve.
words.ex: The mountain town's water shortage seemed intractable until engineers proposed a new reservoir.
words.ex2: The intractable mule planted its hooves and refused to cross the stream.
words.nonExample: A puzzle that a child solves in one minute is not an intractable problem.

morph.note: The opposite, tractable, means easy to manage; it is rare in everyday speech.

apps.academic: Leaders sometimes call a long-running conflict intractable when no plan has worked.
apps.spoken: The traffic here feels intractable at five o'clock.
apps.writing: Use intractable for a problem or a stubborn person that resists every attempt.

cloze.s: After years of failed talks, the dispute seemed so ___ that no one believed it could ever be settled.

cloze2.s: The ___ toddler screamed, kicked, and refused every suggestion his parents tried.

misuse.s: The intractable problem was solved in a moment with one easy step.
misuse.why: Intractable means very hard to solve; one easy step shows the opposite.

visual.alt: A bull standing in front of a roadblock.

words.frame: The problem of ___ seems intractable because ___.

passage.title: The Cart That Would Not Climb
paras: At the county science fair, the challenge sounded simple: build a small cart that could pull a heavy load up a wooden ramp. The robotics club met in Mr. Alvarez's room every afternoon, and Priya arrived with an abstract plan full of arrows, labels, and numbers. It showed the forces beautifully, but it did not show a single real wheel.

Building the first cart took one week. Testing it took about five minutes. When Ben switched on the motor, the wheels spun on the smooth ramp and the cart went nowhere. The team had a traction problem. Ben wanted to extract the battery pack from the back of the cart and bolt it near the front. Priya disagreed. "That would take weight off the drive wheels," she said. "If we subtract the heavy camera from the front instead, the back wheels will press down harder."

The argument became a protracted one. Every afternoon, something new threatened to distract them: a fire drill, a missing screwdriver, a rumor that another school's cart was already finished. On Thursday, Ben finally retracted his claim. "I said the battery belonged up front," he admitted. "I take it back."

Mr. Alvarez refused to hand over an answer. "This only feels intractable because you are arguing instead of testing," he said. "Glue strips of rubber around the wheels and measure what happens." He also warned that the cold gym would make the metal axles contract by a tiny amount, so they should recheck every wheel before the next trial.

On Friday the cart climbed the ramp slowly but steadily, towing a full box of books. The rubber strips had given the wheels the grip they needed. A few scratches on the paint did not detract from the team's pride. Priya looked at her first drawing again and laughed. The abstract plan had been useful, but the real cart had taught them far more.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "protracted" most nearly means
qs.why: The argument runs through several afternoons and is repeatedly interrupted, so it is long and drawn out.

qs.q: Why does Mr. Alvarez say the problem only feels "intractable"?
choices: He thinks the cart design is impossible to fix.
He believes the team is arguing when it should be testing ideas.
He wants the students to give up and try a new project.
He is angry that the gym is too cold for the experiment.
qs.why: He tells them to glue on rubber and measure what happens, which shows the obstacle is the arguing, not the problem itself.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Ben changed his mind?
choices: He switched on the motor during the first test.
He said, "I take it back," about his claim that the battery belonged up front.
He watched the wheels spin on the smooth ramp.
He heard a rumor about another school's cart.
qs.why: Ben openly withdraws his earlier claim, which is what the word retracted describes.

qs.q: In the passage, the "traction problem" refers to
choices: a disagreement between two team members
wheels that could not grip the ramp
a battery that kept running out of power
qs.why: The wheels spin on the smooth ramp and the cart goes nowhere, so the trouble is a lack of grip.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Testing a real idea can solve what arguing and planning alone cannot.
Every science fair challenge is impossible without extra weight.
Teachers should always give students the answer right away.
A first drawing is always better than the finished cart.
qs.why: The problem is solved only after the team tests rubber on the wheels, and Priya admits the real cart taught them more than the plan.

write.prompt: Describe a problem you or your team once solved by testing instead of arguing. Use at least three words from this unit.
write.frame: At first the problem seemed ___, but when we ___, we learned ___.

study.task: Pick three words from the unit and split each into prefix plus tract. Explain in your own words how the prefix steers the pulling (away, out, back, together), then write one sentence for each word that a classmate could not fill with a different tract word.

groups.label: ideas, grip, and problems that resist

shades.label: how easy a problem is to manage

Write a sentence that uses both subtract and difference.

given: The rails were made of metal.
The cold night made them shrink.
combine.model: The metal rails contracted in the cold night, so small gaps appeared between them.

given: The two sides argued for months.
combine.model: The two sides held protracted talks that went nowhere, because the dispute seemed intractable.

discuss: Choose one abstract word such as fairness or loyalty. What concrete example would make it clear to a younger student?
When should a person retract a statement, and when should they stand by it?
Why might a problem feel intractable at first and seem much smaller later? Use two words from the unit.
produce.explain: Explain how the prefixes in retract, extract, and contract change the picture of pulling. Use all three words.

argue.prompt: Claim: Schools should ban phones during class because they distract students. Take a side and support it with two reasons using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. Another reason is that ___ can distract ___.

constructed.prompt: A friend's science poster has strong research but a messy layout. Explain how the layout could affect readers, using distract and detract.
look: names a specific flaw in the layout
explains the effect on the reader without saying the research is bad
constructed.model: The crooked headings and clashing colors distract readers from the data, and they detract from what is otherwise careful research. A cleaner layout would let the evidence stand out.

constructed.prompt: Describe a long argument that ended when one person took something back. Use retract and protracted and say what changed.
look: shows that the argument was long
shows what was taken back and why
constructed.model: The two cousins had a protracted argument about the map. It ended when Leo retracted his claim that the road was open, because the sign proved it was closed.

constructed.prompt: Explain how a good idea can gain traction. Include an abstract idea and a concrete example that helps it spread.
look: gives a concrete example that helps the idea catch on
constructed.model: Fairness is an abstract idea, but it gained traction in our class when we posted a chart showing how many turns each student had on the computers. Seeing the numbers made it real.

teacher.overview: Students use the root tract (pull, draw) and nine prefixes and suffixes to unlock ten words, read a short narrative in which a team solves a traction problem, and practice choosing between close pairs such as retract and detract. The strongest transfer is the habit of splitting an unfamiliar word into prefix plus root and testing the guess against context.

notes.va.distract.v: Most students know this word; push on the structure: dis- (apart, away) plus tract. Ask what is being pulled (attention). Keep the verb and the noun distraction separate in sentences.
notes.va.subtract.v: Easy for students to define but good for showing sub- plus tract. Avoid a made-up story of origin; the sentence 'tract still means pull' is enough. Contrast with add using a two-column chart.
notes.va.extract.v: Two senses: the verb (pull out) and the noun extract (a passage). Stress shifts, which helps students hear the difference. Have students decide which sense each of three sentences uses.
notes.va.retract.v: Pair with detract on one chart: re- is back, de- is down or away. Students often swap them. Use a sentence frame for each and have partners explain which prefix fits.
notes.va.detract.v: Almost always used with from. Contrast with distract: distract moves attention; detract lowers value. Use a rubric example: a typo that detracts from an essay.
notes.va.contract.v: Teach the verb sense (shrink, tighten) first, then show the noun (agreement) as a separate sense with different stress. Students often hear contract and think only of paperwork.
notes.va.abstract.adj: Abstract is a sense-boundary word: an idea (this unit) versus abstract art and an abstract summary. Ask students to sort twelve nouns into abstract and concrete.
notes.va.traction.n: Begin with the physical grip, then show the figurative sense 'gain traction' with a petition or club idea. Link to tractor as a related word, without claiming more about its history.
notes.va.protracted.adj: Shows pro- (forward) in a stretched-out sense. Students confuse it with prolonged-meaning words like 'practiced' or with 'protected'. Use a timeline to show length.
notes.va.intractable.adj: Build from in- (not) plus tract plus -able. The opposite tractable is rare; it is enough to say manageable. Use it for people, problems, and conflicts.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see tract in retract and detract. Tract means pull. Re- means back, so retract pulls a statement back. De- can mean down or away, so detract pulls something down; it lowers how good it seems. The sentence says a few typos should not do that to an argument, so detract fits.'
discuss: Which tract word would you use for a grip that stops a wheel from slipping, and what picture does it call up?
How can the same root give us both extract and contract, which almost sound like opposites?
misconceptions: Every word with tract in it means 'pulling' in a literal way.
Contract only means a written agreement.
extend: Hunt for tract words in a science or history chapter and sort them by prefix.
Write a short scene in which a character must retract a claim and then extract a promise from a friend.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Return to retract/detract and distract/detract as contrast pairs after two days and again at one week; use them whenever students write about a conflict or revise a draft. Revisit mediate, impasse, and escalate by asking students to describe a stalled debate in two sentences.

frames: I can tell the word is about pulling because ___.
___ distracts me from ___, but ___ helps me focus.
wida.oral: Partner A acts out or describes one tract word without saying it (for example, pulling a splinter out); Partner B names the word and the prefix that steers the pull.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (restar, desmerecer, retractar, contraerse, prolongado, intratable) not reviewed by a native speaker; check whether retractar covers both senses of retract and whether prolongado is a cognate of protracted.
Meanings given for sub- ('under; from below') and de- ('down; away') are simplified teaching glosses; no origin claims are made for them.
Passage science claims: removing front weight shifts more weight over the drive wheels, and metal contracts slightly when cooled; confirm wording is acceptable for a grade 7 audience.
